name: Residential capture model scale
consequences: Expanding the residential capture model increases participant throughput and data yield, accelerating method validation and longitudinal phenotyping. The trade-off is higher capital and staffing demands, and potential strain on quality controls if onboarding and training do not scale in parallel.
options: Expand to a 12-suite footprint only after predefined data-quality milestones are met and staffing ratios validated in a dry-run, ensuring operational resilience before scaling.
Optimize eight-suite operations with a modular room reconfiguration plan that can add two additional suites within six weeks if early data show stable throughput.
Maintain eight suites and implement a rigorous process-review to prioritize workflow efficiency, recruitment criteria tightening, and enhanced event-triage accuracy before any expansion.
review: Expansion creates greater throughput but increases capital and staffing pressures; the options do not address long-term sustainability of quality controls and staff fatigue under sustained growth.

name: Data governance and privacy framing
consequences: Pulling this lever reshapes access, sharing, and auditing of data, strengthening privacy and compliance. The downstream implication is slower collaboration and longer turnarounds for external validation while governance processes mature.
options: Adopt a strict de-identification protocol and access controls to align with privacy constraints, enabling broader, safer data sharing while risking reduced granularity for researchers.
Establish a tiered data access framework with researcher-reviewed requests and data-use agreements, balancing openness with participant privacy and practical data-anonymization challenges.
Pilot on-site data governance with automated auditing and consent-tracking to ensure compliance, while implementing governance delays that may slow data release and collaboration.
review: Privacy protections slow data sharing and complicate multi-site collaboration, and the three options do not resolve how to harmonize anonymization standards across collaborators or how to audit data provenance efficiently.

name: Semi-automated event-triage tooling
consequences: Implementing semi-automated triage improves reliability of event labeling and reduces manual review workload. A potential downside is slower adaptation to new or rare patterns if systems rely on established rules or require extensive retraining.
options: Develop a rule-based event-triage pipeline that flags likely parasomnia events and routes to dual human scoring, prioritizing transparency and reproducibility over raw speed.
Implement a learning-enhanced triage module trained on annotated data with regular recalibration, prioritizing accuracy but requiring larger data sets and extended validation.
Leverage ensemble scoring combining sensor streams with clinical metadata to reduce false positives while preserving interpretability for clinicians.
review: Trade-off centers on accuracy gains versus adaptability; the options do not specify how models will remain robust to shifting data distributions and new event morphologies across participants.

name: Night-shift staffing and safety margin
consequences: Pulling this lever rebalances coverage to maintain safety and data integrity during high-activity periods, but increases training, fatigue risk, and administrative overhead if shifts rotate too rapidly.
options: Adopt a rotating night-shift model with cross-trained technicians to maintain coverage while reducing fatigue, improving safety but increasing training overhead.
Contract external on-call technicians for peak nights to bolster response capacity during high-event windows, reducing staffing burden during low-rate periods.
Invest in a dedicated night-shift coordinator and protocol-driven handover rituals to improve incident response while raising administrative coordination complexity.
review: Trade-off between safety coverage and training/coordination overhead; the options do not specify how fatigue will be systematically managed across extended pilot.

name: Recruitment and inclusion strategy
consequences: Pulling this lever broadens the pool of eligible participants and improves representativeness, but can introduce greater heterogeneity in episode patterns and increase screening burdens.
options: Expand recruitment to national networks and international collaborators to diversify sample, potentially extending recruitment timelines but improving generalizability.
Standardize pre-admission tele-screening to quickly assess eligibility, reducing in-person burden while potentially excluding nuanced cases.
Forge formal referral agreements with regional clinics and train staff to collect standardized collateral histories, improving yield from referrals while demanding closer coordination.
review: Expansion improves representativeness but risks longer recruitment pipelines; the options do not address the balance between strict inclusion criteria and practical enrollment speed.

name: Tiered sensing modalities and monitoring cadence
consequences: Tiered sensing increases data richness by layering low-burden nightly monitoring with scheduled enhanced nights, while preserving participant comfort. The trade-off is added maintenance, calibration, and scheduling complexity.
options: Maintain nightly low-burden monitoring with dry-electrode EEG headbands and mattress sensors, ensuring participant comfort and high retention.
Schedule enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage on specific nights to capture diagnostic detail while preserving routine sleep burden for most nights.
Implement escalation nights triggered by technician flags to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution, balancing data richness with scheduling flexibility.
review: Trade-off lies between data richness and participant burden; the options do not specify clear escalation thresholds that prevent overly long stays or participant fatigue.

name: Naturalistic environment fidelity versus safety constraints
consequences: Direct effect: Preserving a domestic ambiance supports natural sleep behavior and participant comfort, boosting ecological validity. Downstream implication: Safety protocols and restricted-opening windows increase intervention latency and staff workload, trading off rapid emergency responsiveness for data realism.
options: Maintain a home-like suite layout while deploying automated fall-detection and real-time alert systems to enable rapid intervention when needed.
Implement a modular safety protocol that can temporarily upgrade to clinical fixtures on high-risk nights to preserve data quality without constant clinicalization.
Adopt a staged ambiance strategy with routine safety drills and increased staff presence during observations to balance ecological validity with reliable emergencies.
review: Trade-off: realism may erode rapid intervention capabilities; gap: none of the options specify exact staffing or budget thresholds required to maintain safety without compromising ecological validity.

name: Adaptive sensing tier allocation
consequences: Direct effect: tailoring sensing intensity reduces participant burden and data load, improving study compliance and processing efficiency. Downstream implication: increased complexity of data integration and potential gaps if thresholds are mis-specified or misapplied across participants.
options: Implement real-time sensor allocation that ramps up data capture only when live indicators suggest risk of events.
Run scheduled calibration windows to reallocate sensors based on annotation throughput and storage limits.
Adopt a mixed-sensor approach with continuous low-burden streams for all participants while deploying episodic high-fidelity PSG on confirmed events.
review: Trade-off: miscalibrated thresholds can miss events or inflate false positives; gap: lacks explicit criteria for threshold setting, validation, and cross-participant consistency.

name: Evidence-driven expansion gating
consequences: Direct effect: expansion proceeds only after predefined data quality and safety KPIs are achieved, reducing premature scaling. Downstream implication: this gating can slow growth and morale if milestones prove hard to reach, potentially affecting funding momentum.
options: Adopt a formal milestone-based expansion plan where additional suites unlock only after predefined data quality and safety KPIs are met.
Accelerate expansion by conducting a parallel pilot in a neighboring facility to validate metrics before Bonn scale-up.
Delay expansion until cost-performance alignment is demonstrated by independent audits and external review.
review: Trade-off: growth is gated and may delay impact; gap: lacks explicit thresholds for what constitutes acceptable data quality and safety performance.

name: Human-in-the-loop adjudication workflow redesign
consequences: Direct effect: prioritizes accuracy while reducing backlog by routing uncertain cases to senior raters; downstream implication: increased cognitive load on senior scorers and potential bottlenecks if escalation capacity is insufficient.
options: Institute a tiered review process where junior scorers flag potential events for senior raters, reducing backlog.
Implement randomized double scoring on a subset to estimate inter-rater reliability and adjust training.
Centralize adjudication with time-boxed review windows to ensure timely scoring while preserving accuracy.
review: Trade-off: efficiency gains may come at the cost of consistency if senior reviewers are overloaded; gap: no defined target for acceptable inter-rater reliability.

name: Participant safety and emergency response architecture
consequences: Direct effect: formalizes response times and escalation paths, reducing risk during events. Downstream implication: higher staffing requirements and potential rigidity limit scheduling flexibility and data-collection variety.
options: Establish a dedicated on-site emergency response protocol with predefined escalation pathways and staff rotation to minimize response latency.
Develop a risk-based staffing framework that adjusts coverage levels based on participant risk profiles and observed event frequency.
Create a drill schedule and incident logging system that trains staff and documents learning for continuous improvement.
review: Trade-off: safety-driven staffing increases fixed costs and may constrain trial flexibility; gap: lacks explicit criteria for triggering staffing adjustments or drill frequency.

name: Prioritization of data streams and archival policy
consequences: Direct effect: defines which streams receive higher fidelity storage and processing, enabling focused analyses. Downstream implication: potential biases in data coverage and reduced availability of lower-priority streams for secondary analyses.
options: Define a data tiering plan that prioritizes high-resolution EEG streams for a subset of nights while maintaining baseline records for all participants.
Implement on-site preprocessing to compress and anonymize data before transfer to university storage, reducing bandwidth needs.
Establish a policy for real-time quality checks and automated metadata tagging to improve later manual scoring efficiency.
review: Trade-off: selective fidelity may bias outcomes if not balanced; gap: lacks criteria for deciding which nights or participants receive higher fidelity data.

name: Escalation-night protocol harmonization
consequences: Pulling this lever tightens escalation-night procedures to yield richer event data during clinically flagged nights, while increasing staff fatigue and scheduling overhead across the unit. A downstream implication is that non-escalation nights may face slower response times or reduced protective coverage if staffing becomes stretched, potentially impacting safety margins and study consistency.
options: Institute a tiered escalation-night protocol that triggers full PSG when predefined cues appear, coordinating schedule and staffing accordingly to improve data richness.
Pilot real-time rule-based event tagging to reduce unnecessary escalations while maintaining data integrity and clinician oversight.
Restructure night-shift schedules to concentrate escalation-night duties on peak-event windows, balancing fatigue with consistent data capture reliability.
review: This lever shifts heavy escalation duties onto staff, improving data during events at the cost of fatigue and complex scheduling; the three options leave unaddressed whether automation can sustain scaling without increasing risk.

name: Continuous annotation throughput optimization
consequences: Pulling this lever reduces backlog and speeds results, but may pressure raters to hurry judgments, risking variability without robust calibration. A downstream implication is that timing gains could erode reliability if ongoing training is neglected.
options: Implement a double-scoring workflow with parallel independent raters during high-load periods to accelerate adjudication while preserving reliability.
Standardize real-time annotation templates and keyboard shortcuts to minimize scorer cognitive load and reduce timing variance across nights.
Cross-train technicians and scorers across roles to quickly reallocate tasks during unexpected staff shortages without compromising data quality.
review: The trade-off is potential consistency risk when distributing workload across multiple raters; the three options do not guarantee durable inter-rater reliability under variable study pace.

name: Collateral history integration and consent governance
consequences: Pulling this lever enriches event-context data and strengthens recruitment accuracy, but it risks introducing selection bias if collateral availability unevenly maps to participant demographics. A downstream implication is that data richness could come at the expense of broader representativeness.
options: Integrate bed-partner collateral history interviews into eligibility screening and consent processes to strengthen event-context data and improve inclusion.
Adopt tiered consent stacking allowing participants to authorize broader data use gradually as trust and familiarity build.
Create a blinded collateral-check protocol that ensures collateral data usage is de-emphasized when consent is limited and bias is minimized.
review: The trade-off is richer contextual data versus recruitment bias; the options omit a clear mechanism to ensure representativeness when collateral availability varies.

name: Environmental design for safety without clinical feel
consequences: Pulling this lever supports naturalistic behavior while preserving safety, but achieving ambiance without compromising visibility or rapid response requires careful balancing and ongoing adjustment. A downstream implication is potential cost pressure and longer setup times for each room, which could constrain scalability.
options: Redesign room layouts to maximize naturalistic behavior while integrating fail-safe features and rapid escape routes clearly marked for safety.
Implement non-intrusive safety monitoring that preserves ambience, such as flexible door alarms and padding, to maintain comfort without compromising detection.
Calibrate acoustic treatment and lighting to minimize arousal without triggering artificial constraints on sleep behavior.
review: Trade-off involves safety margins vs ambient authenticity; none of the options resolve how to uniformly implement room designs across all suites while maintaining safety protocol adherence.

name: Redundant sensor fusion validation against PSG gold standard
consequences: Pulling this lever increases confidence in event mappings by cross-checking streams against PSG benchmarks, improving data interpretation and reliability. A downstream trade-off is higher resource use and longer data processing cycles, which may delay timely insights.
options: Schedule periodic cross-validation sessions where selected nights receive full PSG alongside ongoing in-bed sensors to verify event mappings.
Establish a blinded adjudication subset where certified PSG reviewers compare low-burden streams against full PSG to measure accuracy.
Develop a data reconciliation protocol that flags discordant classifications between sensor streams for joint review and learning.
review: Trade-off is accuracy gain vs resource burden; the options do not specify how to sustain timely analyses if validation cycles lengthen.

name: Adaptive consent architecture for longitudinal stay
consequences: Pulling this lever aligns data-sharing preferences with evolving participant comfort, potentially improving retention and consent accuracy. A downstream implication is regulatory and operational complexity in managing dynamic preferences across multiple streams and timepoints.
options: Offer dynamic consent checkpoints at mid-stay iterations, enabling participants to adjust data-sharing preferences as circumstances evolve.
Pilot opt-in opt-out toggles for specific data streams to empower participant control without disrupting study continuity.
Create feedback loops where consent choices inform future communication strategies and retention incentives to reduce dropout risk.
review: Trade-off is participant autonomy versus governance overhead; the options do not address how to prevent consent drift from weakening data completeness.
